chief_complaint: skin tightening on fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, and sudden severe high blood pressure
hpi_details: 46F with diffuse systemic sclerosis presenting with acute hypertensive crisis (BP 215/135), oliguria, and schistocytes requiring rapid titration of oral ACE inhibitor Captopril.
ideas: She thinks her sudden blood pressure spike and decreased urination are caused by severe stress at work or a bad reaction to an over-the-counter decongestant.
concerns: She is worried that her dangerously high blood pressure will cause a sudden stroke or heart attack, leaving her young children without anyone to care for them.
expectations: She hopes to receive emergency medication to lower her blood pressure safely and have blood tests done to check her kidneys.

available_results.value: Numerous schistocytes consistent with microangiopathic hemolysis

clinical_knowledge.topic: Scleroderma Renal Crisis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Scleroderma Renal Crisis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Scleroderma Renal Crisis Hypertensive Emergency, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: skin tightening on fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, and sudden severe high blood pressure
Key HPI features: 46F with diffuse systemic sclerosis presenting with acute hypertensive crisis (BP 215/135), oliguria, and schistocytes requiring rapid titration of oral ACE inhibitor Captopril.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Scleroderma Renal Crisis Hypertensive Emergency.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Scleroderma Renal Crisis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Blood pressure this severe with new kidney failure in a scleroderma patient — start ACE inhibitor immediately, do not wait.
management_principles: This presentation requires emergency hospital management with immediate nephrology/rheumatology input and closely monitored blood-pressure reduction.
An ACE inhibitor is standard first-line treatment for suspected scleroderma renal crisis, but agent, route, titration, and monitoring must be directed by the inpatient treating team.
Assess creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, CBC/hemolysis markers, ECG/troponin when indicated, neurologic/cardiopulmonary end-organ injury, and possible dialysis need.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Scleroderma Renal Crisis Hypertensive Emergency: skin tightening on fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, and sudden severe high blood pressure. 46F with diffuse systemic sclerosis presenting with acute hypertensive crisis (BP 215/135), oliguria, and schistocytes requiring rapid titration of oral ACE inhibitor Captopril.
reference_soap.objective: BP 215/135 with oliguria and schistocytes is a hypertensive emergency. Obtain repeated monitored BP, creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis, CBC/platelets and hemolysis studies, ECG and evaluation for neurologic, cardiac, and pulmonary end-organ injury.
reference_soap.assessment: Probable scleroderma renal crisis with hypertensive emergency, acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolysis.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Transfer for immediate emergency/inpatient management and urgent nephrology/rheumatology consultation. 2. The treating team should initiate and rapidly titrate ACE-inhibitor therapy with close BP, renal-function, and potassium monitoring. 3. Evaluate for dialysis and alternative thrombotic microangiopathies; seek critical care support for neurologic, cardiac, pulmonary, or worsening renal complications.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Scleroderma Renal Crisis Hypertensive Emergency
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for skin tightening on fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, and sudden severe high blood pressure
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for rheumatology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: In diffuse systemic sclerosis, abrupt severe hypertension with acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolysis suggests scleroderma renal crisis and needs urgent ACE-inhibitor treatment.
red_flags: Severe hypertension with oliguria or new kidney failure requires emergency management

must_ask.say: How long have you had scleroderma, and what type?
Has the amount of urine you're passing decreased?
Have you had a severe headache, vision changes, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

history.answer: I came to the emergency clinic because my blood pressure suddenly spiked up to over 200 today, and I have a terrible pounding headache.
I checked my blood pressure at home this morning because of a severe headache, and the machine read 215 over 135, which has never happened before.
The skin on my fingers has been getting tight and thick over the last four months, and my fingers turn pale and blue in the cold.
The skin tightness started in my fingers, but recently it has spread past my wrists up into my forearms.
My headache is a throbbing, pounding pain at the back of my head, and I would rate it an eight out of ten.
The headache began yesterday afternoon and worsened sharply this morning, while the skin tightness has been slowly worsening over four months.
Cold water or cold air triggers painful white and blue color changes in my fingers, but nothing seems to relieve this headache.
Whenever my hands get cold, my fingers turn completely white and numb, then turn blue, and finally turn red and throb when warmed up.
I noticed that I have barely passed any urine in the past two days, just a few dark drops this morning.
My vision has been blurry and hazy since this morning, but I have not had any seizures or trouble speaking.
I feel a slight tightness in my chest and feel a bit winded when moving around, but I do not have severe tearing pain.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I have not noticed any unusual bruising, purple spots on my skin, or unexpected bleeding.
I felt slightly nauseated this morning because of the terrible headache, but I have not vomited or had diarrhea.
My blood pressure has always been completely normal at my annual checkups, typically around 110 over 70.
I took two acetaminophen tablets this morning and rested in a dark room, but it did not help my headache or blood pressure at all.
I have not taken any decongestants, cold medicines, herbal supplements, or illicit substances, and I have not traveled recently.
I was unable to go to work today because of the pounding headache and dizziness, and my stiff fingers make typing very difficult.
A rheumatologist diagnosed me with diffuse systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, two months ago.
I thought my blood pressure must have skyrocketed from extreme work stress, or maybe from an over-the-counter medicine I took recently.
My blood pressure numbers are through the roof, and I'm terrified I'll have a stroke or heart attack and leave my kids on their own.
I'm hoping you can give me emergency medication right away to get my blood pressure down and check my kidneys to make sure they aren't damaged.
Other than the recent diagnosis of scleroderma, I have never had chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I had my appendix removed when I was twenty years old, but I have had no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I am not currently taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, steroids, or health supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink a single glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and nothing more.
I work full-time as an accountant and live at home with my husband and two teenage children.
My mother had rheumatoid arthritis, but there is no family history of kidney disease or early high blood pressure.
My last period was two weeks ago with regular cycles, and I had a tubal ligation ten years ago, so there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Alert, middle-aged female appearing in moderate distress from a severe headache, sitting upright.
Blood pressure 215/135 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Pupils equal and reactive to light; fundoscopic examination shows bilateral flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and papilledema.
Tachycardic rhythm with prominent S4 gallop; no murmurs, friction rubs, or pericardial knock.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds; no crackles or wheezes.
Soft and non-distended, non-tender to light and deep palpation without guarding or organomegaly.
Trace bilateral pitting pretibial edema; no cyanosis or clubbing of lower extremities.
Thickened, taut, and shiny skin with loss of normal skin folds over fingers, hands, and distal forearms, with sclerodactyly and flexion contractures; no petechiae, purpura, or active digital ulcers.
Alert and fully oriented to person, place, and time; cranial nerves II-XII grossly intact with no focal neurologic deficit.
